set1.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set1.q: A 52-year-old man has crushing chest pain. His 12-lead is shown. Occlusion of which artery best explains the pattern in V1 to V4?
opts: Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery supplies the right atrium, right ventricle and bottom of the left ventricle; its occlusion shows up in II, III and aVF, not V1 to V4.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the side and back of the left ventricle; its territory shows in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) or as posterior changes.
Left anterior descending
Correct. ST elevation in V1 to V4 involves the septal and anterior walls, which the left anterior descending artery supplies (front of the left ventricle and front of the septum).
A coronary vein
The coronary veins carry used, deoxygenated blood from the heart muscle back to the right atrium; an arterial occlusion causes this pattern.
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set1.q: A 63-year-old woman has an anteroseptal infarction. Which leads make up the anteroseptal territory?
opts: V3, V4, V5 and V6
V5 and V6 are lateral leads; the anteroseptal territory is V1 to V4.
II, III and aVF
II, III and aVF are the inferior leads, viewing the bottom of the left ventricle, not the septum.
V1, V2, V3 and V4
Correct. The anteroseptal territory is V1 to V4: the septal leads V1 and V2 plus the anterior leads V3 and V4, with no reciprocal leads.
I, aVL, V5 and V6
I, aVL, V5 and V6 are the lateral leads, the circumflex territory, not the anteroseptal one.

set1.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set1.q: A 42-year-old man has chest pain and the 12-lead shown. Which region of the heart does the ST elevation localize to?
opts: High lateral wall
The high lateral wall is viewed by I and aVL. On this tracing those leads show ST depression, the reciprocal of the inferior elevation.
Anteroseptal wall
The anteroseptal wall is viewed by V1 to V4. Elevation there would sit in the chest leads, not in II, III and aVF.
Inferior wall
Correct. The ST elevation is in II, III and aVF, contiguous leads that look at the inferior region, so this is documented as an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
Posterior wall
No standard lead faces the posterior wall; it shows as isolated ST depression in V1 to V4 and is confirmed with V7 to V9.
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set1.q: A 67-year-old woman's 12-lead is shown, with ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Which leads carry the reciprocal ST depression?
opts: Leads I and aVL
Correct. I and aVL are the reciprocal leads of the inferior wall, and here they show the mirror-image ST depression that confirms the inferior infarction.
Leads V1 to V3
Isolated depression in V1 to V3 is the mirror of a POSTERIOR infarction. The inferior wall's reciprocal leads are I and aVL.
Leads V5 and V6
V5 and V6 face the lateral wall; on the localization table the inferior wall's reciprocal leads are I and aVL only.
Leads II, III and aVF
II, III and aVF are the leads facing the infarct and carry the elevation; reciprocal leads are the opposite ones.
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with a recent infarction has this complex in V2: a single deep negative deflection with no R wave. In this setting, what is it called?
opts: A delta wave
A delta wave is a slurred upstroke at the start of a QRS in preexcitation; it is followed by the rest of a positive QRS.
A pathologic Q wave
Correct. With no R wave the deflection is technically a QS complex, and in the setting of an infarction it is read as a pathological Q wave with no R wave.
An inverted U wave
A U wave follows the T wave and is small; this is the whole ventricular complex, a single deep negative deflection.
A hyperacute T wave
A hyperacute T wave is a broad, tall, upright T wave. This deflection is the QRS itself, deep and negative.
set1.alt: A single electrocardiogram complex on grid paper

set1.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set1.q: A 54-year-old man has ST elevation in V1, V2 and V3. Which walls do these contiguous leads look at?
opts: Inferior and posterior walls
The inferior wall is II, III and aVF, and the posterior wall has no facing lead on the standard tracing.
Anterior and septal walls
Correct. V1, V2 and V3 are contiguous leads looking at the anterior and septal walls, an anteroseptal infarction.
High lateral wall
The high lateral wall is viewed by I and aVL, not by the chest leads V1 to V3.
Right ventricle
The right ventricle is viewed by a right-sided lead such as V4R, not by V1 to V3.

set1.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
set1.q: A 68-year-old woman is told the artery that supplies the back of her septum is blocked. Which artery is it?
opts: Left anterior descending
The left anterior descending artery supplies the FRONT of the septum; the back of the septum belongs to the right coronary artery.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle, not the septum.
Coronary veins
The coronary veins drain used blood to the right atrium; the septum is supplied by arteries.
Right coronary artery
Correct. The right coronary artery supplies the back of the septum along with the right atrium, the right ventricle and the bottom portion of the left ventricle.

set1.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set1.q: A 72-year-old man has an inferior infarction. Which findings should raise suspicion of right ventricular involvement?
opts: Hypotension, clear lungs, raised neck veins
Correct. Right ventricular involvement should be suspected whenever a patient with acute coronary syndrome symptoms presents with hypotension, clear lung sounds and jugular vein distension.
Hypertension, crackles, leg swelling
The triad for right ventricular involvement is hypotension, CLEAR lungs and distended neck veins; crackles are the opposite of clear lungs.
Fever, cough and pleuritic pain
These do not identify right ventricular involvement; the cue is hypotension with clear lungs and jugular vein distension.
Bradycardia alone, normal pressure
Bradycardia alone does not define it; the triad is hypotension, clear lung sounds and jugular vein distension.

set1.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set1.q: A 64-year-old woman has chest pain and the 12-lead shown. Which region does the ST elevation localize to?
opts: Inferior wall
The inferior leads (II, III, aVF) show depression on this tracing; that is the reciprocal of the high lateral elevation, not the infarct itself.
Anteroseptal wall
Anteroseptal infarction elevates V1 to V4; the elevation that localizes this infarct is in I and aVL, with reciprocal depression in III and aVF.
Right ventricle
Right ventricular involvement is confirmed by ST elevation in V4R on a right-sided tracing; it is not what I and aVL show.
High lateral wall
Correct. ST elevation in I and aVL, contiguous leads looking at the high lateral wall of the left ventricle, with reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF.
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of myocardial ischemia and infarction.
set1.q: A 64-year-old man with no known heart history has a complex like this in leads II, III and aVF. What does the deep first deflection represent?
opts: Reversible ischemia
Reversible ischemia shows as hyperacute T waves or ST depression. A pathologic Q wave means tissue has already died.
Transmural injury in progress
Injury (transmural ischemia) is shown by ST elevation. The Q wave marks infarction, the stage after injury.
Death of myocardial tissue
Correct. Pathological Q waves represent infarction, the actual death of cardiac tissue, from either a previous or an acute cardiac event.
Normal septal activation
A normal septal Q wave is small and shallow; one this deep, past 2 mm and a quarter of the R wave's height, meets the pathologic criteria.
set1.alt: A single electrocardiogram complex on grid paper

set1.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
set1.q: A 63-year-old man asks how blood leaves the heart muscle once it has been used. Which vessels return it to the right atrium?
opts: The coronary arteries
The coronary arteries deliver oxygenated blood to the myocardium; it is the coronary veins that return the used blood.
The coronary veins
Correct. The coronary veins take oxygen-poor blood that the heart muscle has already used and return it to the right atrium.
The pulmonary arteries
The pulmonary arteries carry blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, not from the myocardium to the right atrium.
The vena cava
The vena cava returns blood from the body. The heart muscle's own used blood drains through the coronary veins.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: myocardial ischemia, myocardial injury, myocardial infarction
set1.q: A 48-year-old man has had 20 minutes of chest pressure. His precordial leads are shown, with no ST elevation. What are these T waves?
opts: Normal T waves
Normal T waves are asymmetrical, with a slow initial upstroke and a sharper terminal downstroke, and their amplitude is modest. These are tall and symmetrical.
Inverted T waves
These T waves point upward. T-wave inversion is a later ischemic sign than hyperacute T waves.
Hyperacute T waves
Correct. Tall, increased in amplitude and symmetrical, with no ST elevation yet: hyperacute T waves, often the very first sign of cardiac ischemia.
Flattened T waves
Flattened T waves (a hypokalemia and hypothyroidism finding) are low and shallow; these are tall and upright.
set1.alt: Six precordial leads, V1 to V6, on grid paper

set1.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set1.q: A 55-year-old man has chest pain and the 12-lead shown. Which region does the ST elevation in V1 to V3 localize to?
opts: Anteroseptal wall
Correct. V1, V2 and V3 are contiguous leads looking at the anterior and septal walls, so this is an anteroseptal ST-elevation infarction.
Inferior wall
The inferior wall is viewed by II, III and aVF; elevation there would be in the limb leads, not V1 to V3.
High lateral wall
The high lateral wall is viewed by I and aVL; the leads named here, V1 to V3, face the anterior and septal walls instead.
Posterior wall
A posterior infarction shows as ST DEPRESSION in V1 to V4 on the standard tracing; elevation in V1 to V3 faces the anteroseptal wall directly.
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of myocardial ischemia and infarction.
set1.q: A 71-year-old man with exertional chest pain has the 12-lead shown. Which layer of the heart does this pattern indicate is ischemic?
opts: The full wall thickness
Ischemia through the full wall thickness is transmural ischemia, also called injury, and it produces ST-segment elevation rather than depression.
The epicardium alone
The epicardium lies next to the coronary arteries and is the best perfused layer. Subendocardial ischemia, shown as ST depression, affects the innermost layer.
The subendocardium
Correct. Global ST-segment depression represents subendocardial ischemia: the innermost layer, farthest from the epicardial coronary arteries, is starved first.
The pericardium
Inflammation of the pericardium (pericarditis) gives global concave ST elevation with PR depression, not the diffuse ST depression shown here.
set1.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 8; tracing from Slide 9
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
set1.q: A 68-year-old man has a Q wave in lead III. Which duration makes a Q wave pathologic?
opts: Longer than 0.02 seconds
Half a small box is too short a threshold. The pathologic duration is longer than 0.04 seconds, one small box.
Longer than 0.04 seconds
Correct. A pathological Q wave is longer than 0.04 seconds in duration, one small box, and deeper than 2 mm (or more than 25% of a following R wave).
Longer than 0.12 seconds
Three small boxes is a QRS width threshold, not the Q-wave criterion, which is longer than 0.04 seconds.
Longer than 0.20 seconds
One large box is the upper limit of the PR interval; a Q wave is pathologic when longer than 0.04 seconds.

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: myocardial ischemia, myocardial injury, myocardial infarction
set1.q: A healthy 30-year-old woman's T waves are shown. If ischemia began, which change in these T waves is often the very first sign?
opts: They become inverted
T-wave inversion is a sign of ischemia, but it comes later than hyperacute T waves.
They become flattened
Flattened T waves belong to hypokalemia and hypothyroidism, not to the first minutes of ischemia.
They disappear entirely
The T wave does not vanish with ischemia; the earliest change is that it grows broad, tall and symmetrical.
They become hyperacute
Correct. Hyperacute T waves, broad, increased in amplitude and symmetrical, are often the very first sign of cardiac ischemia; the normal T wave shown is asymmetrical.
set1.alt: A single-lead rhythm strip on grid paper

set1.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
set1.q: A 45-year-old man's tracing is being measured for ST changes. Where is the J point?
opts: End of the QRS, start of ST
Correct. The junction point, or J point, lies between the QRS complex and the ST segment; ST deviation is judged at this point.
Where the T wave ends
The end of the T wave marks the end of repolarization. The J point is the junction at the end of the QRS.
Where the P wave begins
The start of the P wave is atrial depolarization; the J point sits at the end of the QRS complex.
At the peak of the R wave
The R-wave peak is within the QRS; the J point is where the QRS ends and the ST segment begins.

set1.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of myocardial ischemia and infarction.
set1.q: A 59-year-old man has ST-segment elevation from transmural ischemia. Through which part of the wall does the ischemia extend?
opts: The innermost layer only
Ischemia confined to the innermost layer is subendocardial ischemia, which shows as ST depression.
The full wall thickness
Correct. Transmural ischemia spans the full thickness of the wall (it is also called injury) and is represented by ST elevation.
The outer epicardium only
The epicardium lies next to the coronary arteries; transmural means across the whole wall, not one layer.
The pericardial sac
The pericardium is outside the myocardium; its inflammation is pericarditis, not transmural ischemia.

set1.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set1.q: A 57-year-old woman with chest pain has ST elevation in II, III and aVF but no reciprocal depression anywhere. How should the missing reciprocal changes be read?
opts: They rule out an infarction
Absence of reciprocal changes is not a rule-out criterion. ST elevation of 1 mm in two contiguous leads defines the infarction with or without them.
They prove lead misplacement
Missing reciprocal changes are common and do not imply a technical error; the elevation still has to be taken seriously.
They confirm benign repolarization
Localized ST elevation in II, III and aVF in a patient with chest pain is not benign; the lack of reciprocal changes does not change that.
They do not exclude ischemia
Correct. Reciprocal changes confirm ischemia when ST elevation is present, but their absence does not exclude cardiac ischemia; an ST-elevation infarction is considered with or without them.

set1.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set1.q: A 62-year-old woman has chest pain. Her 12-lead is shown, with ST depression in V1 to V3 and no ST elevation anywhere. Which is the next best step?
opts: Record right-sided lead V4R
V4R checks for right ventricular involvement in an inferior infarction. The pattern here (isolated anterior depression) calls for the posterior leads.
Repeat the standard 12 leads only
The standard leads have no camera on the back of the heart; repeating them cannot show the posterior wall that this depression may be mirroring.
Treat as anterior ischemia only
Isolated V1 to V4 depression must be presumed reciprocal to a posterior infarction until proven otherwise; settling for anterior ischemia risks missing it.
Record posterior leads V7 to V9
Correct. Isolated ST depression in V1 to V4 with no elevation anywhere is a reciprocal change for a posterior infarction until proven otherwise, so a posterior (15-lead) tracing is obtained.
set1.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 19; tracing from Slide 20
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
set1.q: A 51-year-old woman is told her blocked artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and the front of the septum. Which artery is it?
opts: Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery supplies the back of the septum, the right heart and the bottom of the left ventricle, not the front of the septum.
Left anterior descending
Correct. The left anterior descending artery supplies the front (and bottom) of the left ventricle and the front of the septum, which is why it carries septal and anterior infarctions.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex runs around to the side and back of the left ventricle; it does not supply the front of the septum.
Coronary veins
The coronary veins return oxygen-poor blood to the right atrium. Arteries, here the left anterior descending, supply the muscle.

set1.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set1.q: A 62-year-old man has ST elevation in lead I. Which lead is contiguous with lead I?
opts: aVF
aVF is an inferior lead, contiguous with II and III; it looks from the opposite direction to lead I.
aVL
Correct. I and aVL are contiguous leads that look at the high lateral wall of the left ventricle.
V1
V1 is a septal lead, contiguous with V2; it does not view the high lateral wall.
III
Lead III is inferior, contiguous with II and aVF, and is a reciprocal lead for a high lateral infarction.

set1.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set1.q: A 64-year-old man has an infarction with no facing lead on the standard 12-lead. Which leads carry its reciprocal changes?
opts: V1, V2, V3 and V4
Correct. The posterior wall has no facing lead on the standard 12-lead, and its reciprocal leads are V1, V2, V3 and V4.
II, III and aVF
II, III and aVF face the inferior wall and are the reciprocal leads of a LATERAL infarction.
I and aVL
I and aVL are the reciprocal leads of an INFERIOR infarction.
V5 and V6
V5 and V6 face the lateral wall; the posterior wall mirrors in V1 to V4.

set1.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
set1.q: A 60-year-old man's rhythm strip is shown at a fast rate. Which usual baseline has disappeared, making ST deviation harder to judge?
opts: The PR interval
The PR interval runs from the start of the P wave to the QRS; it is not the reference baseline for the J point, which is the TP segment.
The QRS complex
The QRS is still present on every beat; it is the flat TP segment between beats that has disappeared at this rate.
The ST segment
The ST segment is what is being judged, not the baseline it is compared against; that baseline is the TP segment.
The TP segment
Correct. The TP segment is the usual baseline for judging the J point, but at fast heart rates it can be hard to locate, and the onset of the QRS is used instead.
set1.alt: A single-lead rhythm strip on grid paper at a fast rate

set1.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with an inferior infarction needs lead V4R. Where is it placed?
opts: Left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular
The left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line is the standard V4 position; V4R mirrors it on the right.
On the back below the scapula
Electrodes below the scapula are posterior leads (V7 to V9) for a posterior infarction, not V4R.
Right 2nd intercostal space at the sternum
V4R sits at the fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line, on the right, mirroring the usual V4 position.
Right 5th intercostal space, midclavicular
Correct. V4 is moved to the right side of the sternum, fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line, and the tracing is repeated; the right-sided V4 is marked V4R.

set1.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
set1.q: A 74-year-old woman's right-sided tracing is shown, with ST elevation in V4R during an inferior infarction. Occlusion of which artery explains this?
opts: Right coronary artery
Correct. Inferior infarctions involving the right coronary artery can include the right ventricle, which the right coronary artery supplies along with the right atrium.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the side and back of the left ventricle. It does not supply the right ventricle that V4R views.
Left anterior descending
The left anterior descending artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and septum, not the right ventricle.
Left main coronary artery
The left main feeds the circumflex and left anterior descending arteries; the right ventricle is perfused by the right coronary artery.
set1.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 22; tracing from Slide 24
set1.alt: Electrocardiogram with the V4 label circled and relabeled by hand

set1.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
set1.q: A 50-year-old woman's ST segment is being examined. Where does the ST segment begin and end?
opts: End of P wave to start of QRS
The end of the P wave to the start of the QRS is the PR segment. The ST segment follows the QRS.
J point to the onset of the T wave
Correct. The ST segment begins at the J point and terminates at the onset of the T wave; in a healthy heart it lies at baseline.
Start of QRS to end of T wave
The start of the QRS to the end of the T wave is the QT interval, which contains the ST segment.
End of T wave to next P wave
The end of the T wave to the next P wave is the TP segment, the baseline used to judge the ST segment.

set1.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set1.q: A 62-year-old woman's 12-lead is being read wall by wall. Which lead is not assigned to any wall?
opts: aVL
aVL is assigned to the lateral wall; with lead I it views the high lateral wall of the left ventricle.
aVF
aVF is assigned to the inferior wall, together with II and III, the inferior leads.
aVR
Correct. On the localization table every lead is given a wall (lateral, inferior, septal or anterior) except aVR.
V4
V4 is assigned to the anterior wall, together with V3; V1 and V2 are the septal leads.

set1.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set1.q: A 55-year-old man has ST elevation in two leads. Which pair counts as contiguous leads?
opts: II and aVF
Correct. II, III and aVF are contiguous leads that all look at the inferior region, so II and aVF are contiguous.
V1 and aVL
V1 is a septal lead and aVL a lateral one; they look at different walls and are not contiguous.
II and aVL
II is inferior and aVL is high lateral; they look at opposite walls, which makes them reciprocal, not contiguous.
aVF and V1
aVF is inferior and V1 is septal; leads are contiguous when they look at the same region.

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction.
set1.q: A 64-year-old woman's chart says she has transmural ischemia. Which other term refers to the same thing?
opts: Myocardial injury
Correct. Transmural ischemia is also referred to as injury, and it is represented on the tracing by ST-segment elevation.
Subendocardial ischemia
Subendocardial ischemia is confined to the inner layer and shows as ST depression; transmural ischemia spans the full wall.
Pathologic Q wave formation
Pathologic Q waves mark infarction, the death of tissue; transmural ischemia is injury, which shows as ST elevation.
Early repolarization
Early repolarization is a benign normal variant of ST elevation, not a synonym for transmural ischemia.

set2.io: Discuss the related anatomy and physiology of myocardial ischemia and infarction.
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman with a recent infarction has this QS complex in V2. What has happened to the tissue under that lead?
opts: It is reversibly ischemic
Reversible ischemia shows as hyperacute T waves or ST depression. Loss of the R wave into a QS complex means the tissue has died.
It is injured but alive
Injury (transmural ischemia) is shown by ST elevation. A pathologic Q wave marks the stage after injury, tissue death.
It is normal septal tissue
Normal septal activation produces a small, narrow initial deflection with an R wave following; a deep QS complex after infarction is pathologic.
It has died (infarction)
Correct. A pathological Q wave, here a QS complex with no R wave, represents infarction: the cells beneath that lead have died and can no longer depolarize.
set2.alt: A single electrocardiogram complex on grid paper

set2.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
set2.q: A 44-year-old woman asks what the letter J in J point stands for. What does it stand for?
opts: Junction
Correct. The junction point, or J point, is the junction between the QRS complex and the ST segment.
Joint
It is not a joint; the J point is the junction where the QRS complex ends and the ST segment begins.
Jump
Nothing jumps there; J stands for junction, the meeting point of the QRS and the ST segment.
Jugular
Jugular refers to the neck veins (jugular vein distension is a right ventricular sign); J point means junction point.

set2.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set2.q: A 59-year-old man has an isolated posterior wall infarction. About what share of acute myocardial infarctions are isolated posterior infarctions?
opts: Correct. Isolated posterior wall infarctions account for 3% to 4% of all acute myocardial infarctions, typically from left circumflex occlusion or stenosis.
That is ten times too high; isolated posterior infarctions are uncommon, about 3% to 4%.
Under 0.1%
Far too low; isolated posterior infarctions are uncommon but not rare, about 3% to 4%.
About half
Half of all infarctions are not isolated posterior ones; the share is 3% to 4%.

set2.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set2.q: A 60-year-old man needs a posterior tracing. Which electrodes are moved to his back, and what are they relabeled?
opts: V1 to V3, relabeled V7 to V9
V1 to V3 stay on the front; they carry the reciprocal depression. It is V4 to V6 that move to the back.
V4 to V6, relabeled V7 to V9
Correct. To obtain a posterior tracing, leads V4, V5 and V6 are moved to the back of the patient and labeled V7, V8 and V9, and the tracing is repeated.
V4 only, relabeled V4R
Moving V4 alone to the right chest makes V4R, the right-sided lead for the right ventricle, not a posterior tracing.
The limb leads, relabeled V7 to V9
The limb electrodes stay on the limbs. The three lateral chest electrodes are the ones moved to the back.

set2.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set2.q: A 63-year-old woman has ST elevation limited to V1 and V2. Which region of the heart do these leads view?
opts: Anterior wall
The anterior wall is viewed by V3 and V4. V1 and V2 view the septum.
Lateral wall
The lateral wall is viewed by I, aVL, V5 and V6, not by V1 and V2, which are the septal leads.
Inferior wall
The inferior wall is viewed by II, III and aVF; elevation limited to V1 and V2 is septal.
Septal wall
Correct. V1 and V2 are the septal leads; elevation limited to them localizes to the septal wall, which has no reciprocal leads on the standard 12-lead.

set2.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set2.q: A 61-year-old man with chest pain has ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Which criterion defines an ST-elevation myocardial infarction in these leads?
opts: 1 mm in any single lead
One lead is not enough; the elevation must appear in two or more contiguous leads looking at the same region.
1 mm or more in two contiguous leads

Correct. An ST-elevation infarction is considered when there is 1 mm or more of elevation in 2 or more contiguous leads, with or without reciprocal changes. (Leads V2 and V3 carry higher, sex- and age-specific thresholds.)
2 mm in three unrelated leads
Leads must be contiguous (same region). Elevation scattered across unrelated walls does not meet the criterion.
Any elevation with reciprocal changes
Reciprocal changes confirm but are not required; the criterion is at least 1 mm in two or more contiguous leads.

set2.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set2.q: A 58-year-old man has ST elevation in V3 and V4 only. Which region of the heart do these leads view?
opts: Septal wall
The septal leads are V1 and V2. V3 and V4 face the anterior wall.
Lateral wall
The lateral leads are I, aVL, V5 and V6; V3 and V4 sit in front of the anterior wall instead.
Posterior wall
No standard lead faces the posterior wall; it is seen through reciprocal depression in V1 to V4 and confirmed with V7 to V9.
Anterior wall
Correct. V3 and V4 are the anterior leads; together with V1 and V2 they make the anteroseptal territory V1 to V4.

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: myocardial ischemia, myocardial injury, myocardial infarction
set2.q: A 49-year-old woman has chest pain and the 12-lead shown. Besides ST elevation, which early ischemic finding is visible in V1 to V4?
opts: Pathologic Q waves
Pathologic Q waves mark tissue death and are deep and wide initial negative deflections; the striking change in these leads is the size of the T waves.
Inverted T waves
These T waves point upward and are enlarged. T-wave inversion is a different, later sign of ischemia.
Prominent U waves
Prominent U waves are a hypokalemia finding that follows the T wave; here the T wave itself is broad, tall and symmetrical.
Hyperacute T waves
Correct. The T waves are broad, increased in amplitude and symmetrical, large enough to hold the QRS inside them: hyperacute T waves alongside the ST elevation.
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction.
set2.q: A 59-year-old woman's tracings are compared over an evolving infarction. Which pairing of finding and process is correct?
opts: ST depression and transmural injury
ST depression represents SUBENDOCARDIAL ischemia. Transmural injury elevates the ST segment.
ST elevation and transmural injury
Correct. ST elevation represents transmural ischemia, also called injury; ST depression is subendocardial ischemia and Q waves are infarction.
Q waves and reversible ischemia
Pathologic Q waves represent infarction, the death of tissue, not reversible ischemia.
Hyperacute T waves and dead tissue
Hyperacute T waves are often the first sign of ischemia; dead tissue is marked by pathologic Q waves.

set2.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set2.q: A 61-year-old man has ST elevation in I, aVL and V3 to V6. Which region does this localize to?
opts: Anterolateral wall
Correct. I, aVL, V3, V4, V5 and V6 together are the anterolateral leads; the reciprocal leads are II, III and aVF.
Anteroseptal wall
The anteroseptal leads are V1 to V4; the lateral leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 are not part of it.
Inferior wall
The inferior wall is II, III and aVF, which here would be the reciprocal leads.
Septal wall
The septal leads are V1 and V2 only; adding I, aVL and V3 to V6 makes the anterolateral territory.

set2.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set2.q: A 62-year-old woman's posterior tracing has been recorded. Which finding confirms a posterior wall infarction?
opts: ST depression in V7 to V9
Depression is what the FRONT leads show; facing the infarct from behind, the posterior leads show elevation.
ST elevation in V7 to V9
Correct. ST-segment elevation in the posterior leads V7, V8 and V9 is the confirmatory sign of a posterior wall infarction.
Q waves in V1 and V2
Q waves in V1 and V2 would point to septal tissue death, not confirm a posterior infarction.
Hyperacute T waves in V5
A lateral lead's T waves do not confirm the posterior wall; the confirmation is elevation in V7 to V9.

set2.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
set2.q: A 57-year-old man has chest pain and the 12-lead shown, with ST elevation in V1 to V3. Occlusion of which artery best explains it?
opts: Left anterior descending
Correct. The left anterior descending artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and the front of the septum, the anterior and septal walls that V1 to V3 face.
Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery supplies the right heart and the bottom of the left ventricle; its occlusion elevates II, III and aVF, which are depressed here.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle; it does not explain elevation in V1 to V3.
A coronary vein
The coronary veins return used blood to the right atrium; an infarction pattern comes from an arterial occlusion.
set2.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 4; tracing from Slide 18
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set2.q: A 56-year-old man's tracing is described as showing reciprocal changes. What are reciprocal changes?
opts: A second, separate infarction
Reciprocal changes reflect the same event seen from the opposite side, not a second event.
Changes seen only after reperfusion
Reciprocal changes appear during the acute event as the mirror image of the elevation; they are not a reperfusion sign.
A mirror image on the opposite leads
Correct. Reciprocal changes are the mirror image of a cardiac event on the opposite leads, which look at the same area of the heart from the other side.
Artifact from loose electrodes
Reciprocal changes are real physiology, a confirmatory sign of ischemia when ST elevation is present.

set2.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set2.q: A 53-year-old woman with chest pain has these precordial T waves but no ST elevation or depression. Why does this finding matter?
opts: It is a normal variant
Tall, symmetrical T waves in a patient with chest pain are hyperacute, not a variant; normal T waves are asymmetrical and modest.
It is often the first sign of ischemia
Correct. Hyperacute T waves are often the very first sign of cardiac ischemia. Because there is no ST change to call yet, they are easily missed.
It proves an old infarction
An old infarction is shown by pathologic Q waves. Hyperacute T waves come at the very start of an ischemic event.
It shows dead myocardial tissue
Tissue death is marked by pathologic Q waves. Hyperacute T waves appear before injury or infarction has developed.
set2.alt: Six precordial leads, V1 to V6, on grid paper

set2.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set2.q: A 62-year-old woman had V4, V5 and V6 moved to her back and the tracing repeated, as shown. What is this recording often called?
opts: A right-sided electrocardiogram
A right-sided tracing moves V4 to the right fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line (V4R) to look at the right ventricle, not to the back.
A 3-lead rhythm strip
A rhythm strip monitors rate and rhythm in a few leads. The posterior tracing is a full 12-lead with three chest electrodes relocated.
A reversed limb-lead tracing
No limb electrode is moved here; the three lateral chest electrodes are relocated to the back to view the posterior wall.
A 15-lead electrocardiogram
Correct. Moving V4 to V6 to the back as V7, V8 and V9 and repeating the tracing gives what is at times called a 15-lead electrocardiogram, the posterior tracing.
set2.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 19; tracing from Slide 21
set2.alt: Electrocardiogram with three chest-lead labels crossed out and handwritten replacements (V7, V8, V9)

set2.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
set2.q: A 61-year-old man's 12-lead is shown, with ST elevation in I and aVL and reciprocal depression in III and aVF. Occlusion of which artery best explains it?
opts: Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery supplies the right heart and the bottom of the left ventricle; its occlusion elevates II, III and aVF, which are depressed here.
A coronary vein
The coronary veins return used blood to the right atrium; an infarction pattern comes from an arterial occlusion.
Left main coronary artery
A left main occlusion starves both of its branches, so the anterior and septal leads would be elevated too, not the high lateral leads alone.
Left circumflex artery

Correct. The circumflex wraps around to supply the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle, so of these arteries it best explains a lateral infarction (a diagonal branch of the left anterior descending can also cause one).
set2.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 4; tracing from Slide 17
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
set2.q: A 73-year-old woman has an inferior infarction that also involves her right ventricle. Which artery's occlusion causes this combination?
opts: Left anterior descending
The left anterior descending artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and septum, not the right ventricle.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the side and back of the left ventricle, not the right ventricle.
Right coronary artery
Correct. Inferior infarctions involving the right coronary artery can include the right ventricle, because that artery supplies the right ventricle as well as the bottom of the left ventricle.
Left main coronary artery
The left main gives rise to the circumflex and left anterior descending arteries; neither supplies the right ventricle.

set2.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
set2.q: A 60-year-old man is told his left coronary artery divides into two branches soon after it leaves the aorta. Which two?
opts: Circumflex and right coronary
The right coronary artery is a separate vessel from the aorta, not a branch of the left; the left divides into the circumflex and the left anterior descending.
Right coronary and left anterior descending
The right coronary artery arises on its own; the left coronary artery's two branches are the left anterior descending and the circumflex.
Circumflex and left anterior descending
Correct. The left coronary artery divides into two branches: the circumflex artery and the left anterior descending artery.
Coronary veins and coronary sinus
The coronary veins are venous return to the right atrium, not arterial branches; the left coronary artery divides into the circumflex and the left anterior descending.

set2.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
set2.q: A 69-year-old woman's limb leads are shown, with Q waves and ST elevation in III and aVF. Which artery most likely supplies the affected wall?
opts: Left anterior descending
The left anterior descending artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and the front of the septum, which the V leads (V1 to V4) view.
Left circumflex artery
The circumflex supplies the side and back of the left ventricle; its occlusion shows in the lateral leads or as a posterior infarction.
Right coronary artery
Correct. III and aVF view the inferior wall, and the right coronary artery supplies the bottom (inferior) portion of the left ventricle along with the right atrium and right ventricle.
Left main coronary artery
The left main divides into the circumflex and the left anterior descending; it does not supply the inferior wall that III and aVF view.
set2.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 4; tracing from Slide 13
set2.alt: Limb-lead electrocardiogram (leads I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) on grid paper

set2.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set2.q: A 58-year-old man's 12-lead is shown, with ST elevation in II, III and aVF. How should the ST depression in leads I and aVL be read?
opts: As a reciprocal change
Correct. ST depression should always be considered a reciprocal change when ST elevation exists in the same tracing. I and aVL mirror the inferior leads, and the depression confirms the event.
As a second infarction
Reciprocal depression is the mirror image of one event seen from the opposite side, not evidence of a separate infarction.
As lateral subendocardial ischemia
With ST elevation on the same tracing, depression is read as reciprocal first. Global depression without elevation is what points to subendocardial ischemia.
As a lead placement error
Mirror-image depression in the leads opposite an infarct is expected physiology, and it is a confirmatory sign of ischemia, not a technical fault.
set2.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 14; tracing from Slide 16
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
set2.q: A 57-year-old man has ST-segment elevation in II, III and aVF. Which process does the elevation represent?
opts: Subendocardial ischemia
Subendocardial ischemia, confined to the inner layer, is represented by ST DEPRESSION.
Old healed infarction
An old infarction is marked by pathologic Q waves; ST elevation means active injury.
Transmural ischemia (injury)
Correct. ST elevation represents transmural ischemia, ischemia through the full thickness of the wall, which is also referred to as injury.
Normal repolarization
In a healthy heart the ST segment sits at baseline; elevation in contiguous leads with chest pain is injury.

set2.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman has chest pressure at rest. Her 12-lead is shown. Which finding is present across most leads?
opts: ST-segment elevation
ST elevation would put the J point above the baseline in contiguous leads; here it sits below it almost everywhere, which is depression.
Pathologic Q waves
Pathologic Q waves are deep, wide initial negative deflections that mark dead tissue. These complexes begin with normal upstrokes; the change is in the ST segment.
ST-segment depression
Correct. The J point and ST segment sit below the baseline in nearly every lead. Global ST-segment depression is the picture of subendocardial ischemia.
Hyperacute T waves
Hyperacute T waves are broad, tall and symmetrical. The abnormality on this tracing is the ST segment dropping below baseline, not an enlarged T wave.
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: myocardial ischemia, myocardial injury, myocardial infarction
set2.q: A 61-year-old man has myocardial ischemia from an acute coronary syndrome. How can this move his J point?
opts: Above or below the baseline
Correct. Cardiac events such as myocardial ischemia (acute coronary syndrome) can cause depression or elevation of the J point relative to the baseline, called ST elevation or ST depression.
Only above the baseline
Ischemia can push the J point either way: below the baseline as ST depression (subendocardial) or above it as ST elevation (transmural).
Only below the baseline
Ischemia can also raise the J point, as ST elevation from transmural ischemia. Both directions occur.
It never moves the J point
J-point displacement is exactly how ischemia shows on the tracing, as ST elevation or ST depression.

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction.
set2.q: A healthy 30-year-old woman has the rhythm strip shown. Which description fits her T waves?
opts: Broad, tall and symmetrical
Broad, tall, symmetrical T waves are hyperacute T waves, the earliest sign of ischemia; normal T waves are asymmetrical.
Asymmetrical, slow upstroke
Correct. Normal T waves are asymmetrical, with a slow initial upstroke and a sharper negative terminal deflection, and a modest amplitude.
Inverted below the baseline
These T waves are upright. T-wave inversion is an ischemic sign, not the normal shape.
Peaked and narrow
Peaked, symmetric T waves are the early sign of hyperkalemia. A normal T wave rises slowly and falls more sharply.
set2.alt: A single-lead rhythm strip on grid paper

set2.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set2.q: A 66-year-old woman has ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which region does this localize to?
opts: Lateral wall
Correct. I, aVL, V5 and V6 are the lateral leads, and the lateral wall's reciprocal leads are II, III and aVF.
Inferior wall
The inferior wall is viewed by II, III and aVF, which are the reciprocal leads of a lateral infarction.
Anteroseptal wall
The anteroseptal wall is viewed by V1 to V4; elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 is lateral.
Posterior wall
The posterior wall has no facing lead on the standard 12-lead; its reciprocal leads are V1 to V4.

set2.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
set2.q: A 59-year-old man who had an infarction last year has this complex in lead III. What is the deep first deflection?
opts: A pathologic Q wave
Correct. The first negative deflection before the R wave is a Q wave; one deeper than 2 mm, or than a quarter of the R wave's height as this one is, is pathologic, a sign of infarction.
A delta wave
A delta wave is a slurred UPSTROKE of the QRS from preexcitation; this is a deep negative deflection before the R wave.
An S wave
An S wave is a negative deflection that comes AFTER the R wave. The first negative deflection, before the R, is the Q wave.
An Osborn wave
An Osborn (J) wave is a notch at the END of the QRS, seen in hypothermia and early repolarization, not a deep initial deflection.
set2.alt: A single electrocardiogram complex on grid paper

set2.io: Differentiate ECG findings associated with ischemia, injury, and infarction: ST-segment elevation, ST-segment depression, T-wave inversion, pathologic Q waves
set2.q: A 55-year-old woman has chest pain and the fast rhythm strip shown, with no visible TP segment. To judge ST elevation, what should the J point be compared with?
opts: The TP segment
The TP segment is the usual baseline, but at this rate it has disappeared, which is exactly when the onset of the QRS is used instead.
The onset of the QRS

Correct. The J point is normally compared to the TP segment, but at fast rates the TP segment can be hard to find, and it is then appropriate to compare the J point to the beginning of the QRS complex.
The peak of the T wave
The peak of the T wave is not a baseline at all; ST deviation is measured against the resting baseline.
The top of the R wave
The R-wave peak measures QRS amplitude, not ST deviation. A baseline is needed, and here that is the start of the QRS.
set2.alt: A single-lead rhythm strip on grid paper at a fast rate

set2.io: Recognize common ECG patterns associated with acute coronary syndromes.
set2.q: A 70-year-old man has chest pain, hypotension, clear lungs and distended neck veins. His 12-lead is shown. Which is the next best step?
opts: Record posterior leads V7 to V9
Posterior leads answer isolated ST depression in V1 to V4. Hypotension, clear lungs and distended neck veins with an inferior infarct point to the right ventricle.
Record right-sided lead V4R

Correct. This is an inferior ST-elevation infarction, and hypotension with clear lungs and jugular vein distension raises suspicion of right ventricular involvement. Moving V4 to the right (V4R) rules it in or out.
Repeat the standard 12 leads only
The standard 12-lead does not look at the right ventricle in its entirety; only a right-sided lead such as V4R can confirm its involvement.
No more leads; it is inferior only
Hypotension, clear lungs and jugular vein distension in an inferior infarction are the cue to suspect right ventricular involvement, so it cannot be assumed inferior only.
set2.cite: 15. EKG Ischemia and Infarction.pptx, Slide 22; tracing from Slide 23
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Correlate ECG lead changes with anatomic regions of the heart.
set2.q: A 49-year-old man has ST elevation in I and aVL with reciprocal depression in III and aVF. Which region is infarcting?
opts: Inferior wall
The inferior leads III and aVF are depressed here, the reciprocal of a high lateral infarction.
Anteroseptal wall
The anteroseptal wall is viewed by V1 to V4, which are not the leads elevated here.
High lateral wall
Correct. I and aVL are contiguous leads looking at the high lateral wall of the left ventricle, with reciprocal ST depression in the inferior leads III and aVF.
Posterior wall
The posterior wall shows as isolated depression in V1 to V4 with no elevation anywhere.

set2.io: Review coronary artery anatomy and myocardial blood supply.
set2.q: A 66-year-old man is told his blocked artery supplies the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle. Which artery is it?
opts: Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, bottom of the left ventricle and back of the septum.
Left anterior descending
The left anterior descending artery supplies the front of the left ventricle and the front of the septum.
Pulmonary artery
The pulmonary artery carries blood to the lungs; it does not supply the myocardium. The coronary arteries do.
Left circumflex artery
Correct. The circumflex artery supplies blood to the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle, the lateral and posterior walls.
